name: Tara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Tara Alvarez, 43, a junior construction worker doing carpentry and general jobs on site. I live with my partner and two school-age children, and I write the day’s measurements in a pocket notebook so I can check them again after lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What work takes most of your time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carry boards, hold frames, mark cuts and help fit trim while the carpenter checks my work. I like leaving a clean edge, and I often use an AI chat tool to explain a tool or step after I get home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a cleaner material list can keep the crew from making a second trip. I would still have someone check the length against the room before I cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my shift is physical, so a little routine software does not remove the carrying and fitting I do. My bigger worry is that our savings would not last long if work paused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the site days offered and confirm the next week’s start before I leave. If we had a short pay week, I would postpone replacing my old kitchen stool, which still holds together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software change sounds minor for my own tasks. I still worry about the gaps between jobs, because the mortgage continues even when the site is quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you notice first when material arrives on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check whether the boards are damaged and whether the lengths match my notebook. A wrong delivery can stop us before we have finished setting the frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the next week had fewer shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor if another crew needs an extra pair of hands. At home, my partner and I would hold off on a purchase that can wait.

say: I would say **a clean material list** can save the crew a second trip.
I would still ask someone to **check the length** before I cut.
think: I do mostly **physical work**, so routine software does not remove my main tasks.
I have little saved, and **a work pause** would be hard on the household.
do: Keep taking **offered site days** and confirm next week’s start before leaving.
Postpone replacing my **usable kitchen stool** after a short-pay week.
feel: **The change** sounds minor, but job gaps still worry me because the mortgage continues.
S0.quote: A wrong delivery can stop us before we have finished setting the frame.
fieldNote: She expects little change to her **physical work** from a small software update.
**Thin savings** make an ordinary work gap a serious household concern.
She and her partner postpone **optional purchases** when work is slow.

steps.text: Keep taking offered site days and confirm the next week’s start
Delay replacing the kitchen stool while it still works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can sort a list faster, but the crew should compare the list with the building before ordering. I would be open about using it to learn a new tool if someone checks the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already ask AI to explain unfamiliar tools and steps, and that helps me study after work. If it takes over more planning, I could lose some small tasks, but I do not know whether that would change the number of site shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the AI tool to practise reading a material plan, then ask the carpenter to show me the real one on site. I would keep my regular shifts while building up the parts of the trade I can do without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel ready to try more because I use the tool at home already. I would still need another person to check my work, and I cannot afford to learn during unpaid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the AI plan matches the site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the marked dimensions with my own notes and the wall we measured. If there is a mismatch, I would stop and ask the carpenter instead of trusting a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the carpenter to teach you next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to practise setting the trim on one doorway and have the carpenter point out where my cuts are rough. I learn faster when I can see the gap with my own eyes.

say: I would say AI can **sort delivery lists** faster, but we should compare them with the building.
I would be open about **learning tools with AI** if someone checks the result.
think: I already use AI to study **unfamiliar tools** after work.
I could lose small planning tasks, but I do not know whether **site shifts would change**.
do: Use AI to practise reading a **material plan**, then compare it with a real site plan.
Keep taking **regular shifts** while learning trade tasks I cannot yet do alone.
feel: I feel ready to try more, but **unpaid learning** and unchecked work would worry me.
S1.quote: I learn faster when I can see the gap with my own eyes.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** supports learning, though she still relies on a carpenter’s eyes.
She does not assume office changes will automatically reduce **site shifts**.

steps.text: Use AI to learn material plans and practise on the site tablet
Practise setting trim with the carpenter checking each doorway
Keep taking current shifts while learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the thinking part changes in 2028, and robots for site tasks come later. I would not tell anyone that the delay means carpentry is protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do the measurements and plan notes I sometimes help prepare by 2028. The physical parts may last longer, but I cannot know how many workers a builder will keep once jobs are reorganised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask to practise installing trim and checking a door frame. In 2029, I would apply for any suitable junior site opening nearby and keep enough for the mortgage before buying tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a tight window, even though I pick up tools quickly once I can try them. I would take the chance to learn, but I do not know whether an application will lead to steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if your shifts were reduced in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them we may need to postpone a family treat and focus on the regular bills. I would explain that the decision comes from work changing, not from anything they did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use the time before robots arrive to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try to become more accurate at fitting and finishing, with someone checking the job before it is signed off. I would not assume there will be work just because robots arrive three years later.

say: I would say **thinking work changes first**, before robots reach site tasks.
I would not call **carpentry protected** because robots arrive later.
think: I expect AI could do **my measurement notes** by 2028.
I may still have **physical tasks** until robots arrive, but I cannot know how many workers a builder will keep.
do: Practise **trim and frames** with a carpenter before 2028.
Apply in 2029 for **nearby site openings** that fit my junior experience.
feel: **Two years is tight**, even though I learn tools quickly once I try them.
I do not know whether applying will lead to **steady work**.
S2.quote: I would not assume there will be work just because robots arrive three years later.
fieldNote: She identifies the **thinking tasks** that may change before physical work.
Her **2029 applications** are a search, not an assumption that vacancies exist.
Her **small reserve** leaves little room to wait without pay.

steps.text: Practise installing trim and checking door frames before 2028
Apply in 2029 for nearby junior site openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives me time to practise more than one part of carpentry. I would not call that time a guarantee of work after the machines become capable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take the planning and measurement notes I help with by 2031. Robots around 2034 could change the lifting and fitting too, so I need to think about both dates instead of only the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise trim, frames and measuring with a carpenter who can point out what I need to fix. In 2032, I would check what nearby employers hire for before paying for training or applying outside construction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to improve and ask questions before AI arrives. I still feel nervous because the money we have saved would not cover a long wait between site jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the carpenter to watch you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for feedback while I fit the corner trim in a small room. I can see a bad joint once it is in place, but I want someone to catch my error before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide to apply for work outside construction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to know that a specific employer is taking applications and what training they expect. If I only hear that some other field might grow, I would keep learning at my current site.

say: I would say **five years** gives me time to practise more than one part of carpentry.
I would not call the warning a **guarantee of work** after machines improve.
think: I think AI may take my **planning notes** by 2031.
I also expect **robots around 2034** could affect lifting and fitting.
do: Practise **trim, frames and measuring** with a carpenter who gives feedback.
Wait on a **course** until I check local hiring needs in 2032.
feel: **Five years gives room** to improve and ask questions before AI arrives.
My savings would not cover a **long wait** between site jobs.
S3.quote: I can see a bad joint once it is in place, but I want someone to catch my error before then.
fieldNote: She uses the longer warning to practise **specific finish work**.
She would not leave construction for a **vague claim** about another field.
A paid course would need to connect to a **real opening** nearby.

steps.text: Practise trim, frames and measurements with supervised feedback
Wait on a course until local hiring needs are clear in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives us more time to see what work remains and decide what to learn. I would still not tell a junior worker that any trade is safe for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes and planning I sometimes help with may be done by AI in 2036, and robots could reach the site in 2039. My children will be older by then, and I do not know what school or household costs they will have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep practising a new site task when the carpenter has time to teach me. In 2037, I would talk with my partner and our older child about subject choices once they are nearer, rather than guessing their plans now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to improve before the first change and see what employers still want. The mortgage still comes each month, and I do not know whether site work lasts past the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children’s study plans today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would wait until the older child is choosing subjects and ask what they are interested in. By then, we can look at real options instead of trying to predict their whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you do with ten years that you could not do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can add skills a little at a time and see what construction employers are still hiring for. I still need to keep up with the household while I learn, because the extra years do not pay the bills.

say: I would say **a decade gives time** to see what work remains and choose what to learn.
I would not say any trade is **safe for good**.
think: I expect AI to take **my work notes** by 2036, then robots may reach the site in 2039.
**My children** will be older, and their choices may change what our household needs.
do: Keep practising **new site tasks** when a carpenter can teach me.
Talk with my partner and older child about **subject choices** in 2037 when they are closer.
feel: **A decade gives time** to improve and see what employers need.
I still worry about the **mortgage** and whether site work lasts after robots arrive.
S4.quote: I still need to keep up with the household while I learn, because the extra years do not pay the bills.
fieldNote: She values **more time to learn** without treating it as permanent protection.
She waits to discuss study plans until the older child’s **real choices are near**.

steps.text: Practise another site task when supervised learning is available
In 2037, discuss subject choices with partner and older child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I have little time to improve before the first change. Paid practice with someone experienced and steady site shifts would help me more than a course I cannot afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I learn best when I can try a task and see what needs correcting. A careful carpenter can show me the mistake before I make it twice, and that matters more than a screen on its own.

theadlineQuote: A careful carpenter can show me the mistake before I make it twice, and that matters more than a screen on its own.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** with an experienced worker and steady site shifts would help her most.
headlineQuote: A careful carpenter can show me the mistake before I make it twice, and that matters more than a screen on its own.
portrait: Tara is a **43-year-old junior construction worker** supporting her partner and two school-age children.
She has **thin savings** and few nearby alternatives if site shifts disappear.
She uses **AI every day** to learn unfamiliar tools and steps.
She is adaptive, but she still relies on **hands-on feedback** to build trade skill.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time to improve before the first change.
